translation.text:
"Have you come?" I say[e], "Because, sir, I am keeping a station[a]."

"What," he says, "is a station?" I say, "I am fasting, sir." He says, "And what is this fasting that you are fasting?" I say, "As I have been accustomed, sir, so I fast."

He says, "You do not know how to fast to the Lord, nor is this useless fast that you fast to him a fast."

I say, "Why, sir, do you say this?"

He says to me, "I tell you, this is not fasting, the kind you suppose you are fasting to the Lord. Listen to a parable. A vineyard, not having weeds, will give more fruit, not being choked by the weeds[f]. So the servant took up [his tool], dug the vineyard, and pulled up all the weeds that were in the vineyard. And that vineyard became very comely and thriving, having no weeds to choke it.

"After a time the master of the servant [and of the field][b] came and went into the vineyard. And seeing the vineyard well fenced, and even dug, and [all] the weeds pulled out[c], he rejoiced greatly over his servant on account of his deed. Summoning again his friends and his son, the master announced to them the deed the servant had done with his portions[d] which he had received; and they approved all the more that the servant should become co-heir with his son."

footnotes.text: Station (Latin statio): an appointed fast or vigil day in early Christian practice.
The bracketed phrase "[and of the field]" indicates textual uncertainty in the source.
The source shows bracketed or truncated words here; the sense is that all the weeds had been pulled up.
Greek ἐπὶ τοῖς ἐδέσμασιν αὐτοῦ οἷς ἔλαβεν: literally, "upon/with the portions he had received"; i.e., in regard to or using the food portions allotted to him.
Or 'He says to me, "Have you come?"'.
Or 'with the portions[d] he had received'.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Latin loanword statio used in early Christian usage for appointed fast/vigil days. Retaining "station" with a gloss preserves the historical term while making sense in context.
Standard rendering; keeps concrete ethical practice without paraphrase.
Here used as polite address to the angelic shepherd, not to God; "sir" avoids confusion with the divine title while reflecting respect.
Context refers to God; retaining "the Lord" with dative "to" reflects idiom and theological orientation of fasting directed Godward.
Carries the force of "of no advantage"; "useless" is concise and forceful, matching the admonitory tone.
Hermas often signals with a parable; although the lemma isn't explicit in the extant line, the discourse introduces a comparison; "parable" preserves genre.
Standard term; vineyard imagery is central and should not be modernized.
In context of a vineyard being choked, the sense is unwanted growth; "weeds" fits the agrarian metaphor better than "herbs."
Agrarian image of choking by weeds; echoes but does not import NT parable language.
Literal agricultural labor; "dug" is clear and idiomatic.
Describes removing weeds by hand; "pulled up" preserves concreteness.
Perfect passive of χαράσσω; "well fenced" conveys the improved, protected state of the vineyard in accessible English.
Adverb modifying the fencing; "well" keeps it idiomatic alongside "well fenced"; the sense of comeliness is then carried by "very comely" later.
Superlative heightens the description; "very comely" keeps the evaluative tone without modern flourish.
Describes healthy growth; "thriving" reads smoothly in modern English.
Owner/employer over a δοῦλος; "master" pairs with "slave" and fits the household metaphor.
Bonded status is salient to the parable’s reward logic; per project policy, "slave" is preferred when ownership/service is active.
Moral/ethical action; "deed" preserves evaluative nuance.
Refers to items of food received; "portions" conveys the concrete allotments without implying modern military "rations."
Collective approval is in view; "approved" is concise and clear.
Maintains the inheritance metaphor; "co-heir" is idiomatic and theologically transparent.

theological_decisions.issue: Rendering of κύριος in address vs. reference to God
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Render vocative κύριε as "sir" when addressed to the shepherd; render τῷ Κυρίῳ as "to the Lord" when referring to God.
theological_decisions.rationale: Hermas uses κύριε as respectful address to an angelic figure; retaining "sir" avoids conflating the messenger with God, while keeping "the Lord" in the theological claim about fasting indicates the divine referent.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Translate δοῦλος as "slave" in this parable.
theological_decisions.rationale: The parable turns on ownership and inheritance; the shock of a slave becoming co-heir heightens the moral. Project policy favors "slave" where bonded status is salient.

theological_decisions.issue: Dative construction in νηστεύειν τῷ Κυρίῳ
theological_decisions.rationale: The Greek dative marks directionality/beneficiary; "to the Lord" is a literal rendering that emphasizes directed devotion without inserting additional ritual connotations.

theological_decisions.issue: Inheritance metaphor in συγκληρονόμον τῷ υἱῷ
theological_decisions.rationale: "Co-heir" preserves the metaphor and allows later readers to hear echoes of early Christian inheritance language without forcing NT phrasing.

review_passes.summary: The draft handles a heavily corrupted source text well, bridging the lacunae sensibly based on standard editions. However, there is a critical pronoun ambiguity at the end where 'the deed he had done' sounds like the master's action rather than the slave's. Additionally, a minor tense inconsistency ('I said' vs 'I say') and a slight flattening of the syntax regarding the 'useless fast' have been corrected to better reflect the Greek.
issues_found: Mistranslation / Pronoun ambiguity: In the final sentence, 'the master announced to them the deed he had done' makes it sound as though the master performed the deed with the portions. The Greek `τὴν πρᾶξιν αὐτοῦ ἣν ἔπραξεν` refers to the slave. Changing 'he' to 'the slave' restores the unambiguous meaning.

Grammar / Syntax loss: The draft renders `οὐδέ ἐστιν νηστεία αὕτη ἡ ἀνωφελὴς ἣν νηστεύετε αὐτῷ` as 'and this fasting of yours is not fasting to him—it is useless.' The Greek literally reads 'nor is this useless fast which you fast to him a fast.' Preserving the original structure ('nor is this useless fast that you fast to him a fast') maintains the author's rhetorical emphasis.
Consistency: The draft translates the present tense `φημί` as 'I said' in the first verse, but correctly as 'I say' in all subsequent instances. This has been harmonized to 'I say'.

revisions.from: He says to me, "Have you come?"
revisions.rationale: The Greek text begins abruptly with the question ἐλήλυθας; (Have you come?). There is no speaker tag (such as λέγει μοι or φησίν) in the source text here. And that vineyard became very comely and thriving, having no weeds to choke it.

translation.text: "After a time the master of the servant [and of the field] came and went into the vineyard. And seeing the vineyard well fenced, and even dug, and [all] the weeds pulled out, he rejoiced greatly over his servant on account of his deed. Summoning again his friends and his son, the master announced to them the deed the servant had done with his portions which he had received; and they approved all the more that the servant should become co-heir with his son."

base_translation.text: He says to me, "I tell you, this is not fasting, the kind you suppose you are fasting to the Lord. Listen to a parable. A vineyard, not having weeds, will give more fruit, not being choked by the weeds. So the slave took up [his tool], dug the vineyard, and pulled up all the weeds that were in the vineyard. And that vineyard became very comely and thriving, having no weeds to choke it.

translation.text: He said to me, “I tell you, this is not the kind of fasting you think you are doing for the Lord. Listen to this parable. A vineyard without weeds produces more fruit because weeds do not choke it. So the servant took his tool, dug the vineyard, and pulled up all the weeds in it. With no weeds to choke it, the vineyard became beautiful and flourished.”

spob_revision_history.previous_text: He said to me, “I tell you, what you think you are doing for the Lord is not true fasting. Listen to this parable. A vineyard without weeds produces more fruit because weeds do not choke it. So the slave took his tool, dug the soil in the vineyard, and pulled up every weed. With no weeds to choke it, the vineyard became beautiful and flourished.”
spob_revision_history.review_summary: The draft substantially improves readability and its vineyard language faithfully states the image and its causal logic. Revision is needed only in the opening sentence: retain “fasting” as the activity the hearer mistakenly thinks he is doing for the Lord, rather than broadening it to unspecified religious activity or using “true fasting,” which may imply a wider definition than this immediate rebuke states.

translation.text: After some time, the servant’s master[a] came into the vineyard. He saw that it had a good fence, that the ground had even been dug up, and that all the weeds had been pulled out. He was very pleased with his servant because of what he had done. So he again called together his friends and his son and told them what the servant had done with the portions he had received. They agreed even more strongly that the servant should share the inheritance with his son.
